About: Spin & Helicity — Overtake an Electron

Concept
Helicity h = S·p̂ is frame-dependent for massive particles: boost past the electron and its momentum reverses while its spin does not, so h flips sign. Chirality is the Lorentz-invariant label (a left-chiral state is left-chiral in every frame), but a helicity eigenstate is a mixture of both: PR,L = (1±β′)/2 with β′ the electron's signed velocity in the observer's frame — 50 : 50 at rest, so helicity and chirality only coincide as E ≫ mc².
Serves
Intro particle physics / early quantum field theory: why "left-handed neutrino" statements are about chirality, why massive fermions have no invariant handedness, and how p′ = γ(p − βE), E′ = γ(E − βp) drive the flip. Engine-verified anchor: a p = 1 MeV/c electron (E = 1.123 MeV, β = 0.8905) boosted at β = 0.9 has p′ = −24.5 keV/c, E′ = 0.512 MeV, h: +1 → −1; its chiral content is 94.5% R in the lab and 47.6% R in the overtaking frame.
Inquiry
Optionally predict what overtaking does to h, then drag the boost slider across the marked flip point (β = 0.890 at p = 1 MeV/c) and compare the verdict against your choice. Then raise p and watch the chirality bar approach 100% R.
Misconception
"Helicity is intrinsic, like spin." It is not for massive particles: the spin sense on screen never changes, but the momentum arrow reverses in the overtaking frame, so h jumps discontinuously from +1 to −1 — it never fades smoothly through zero.
PrincipleHow it appears here
Predict first, never blockingAn optional three-chip prediction sits above the controls; the sim runs fully without it.
Targeted cognitive conflictThe "stay +1" chip encodes the intrinsic-helicity misconception; its rebuttal appears only when that student crosses the flip.
Invariant vs. varyingThe spin arrow and the ball's rotation sense never respond to the boost slider; p′, h and the chirality bar do — and the bar reads 50 : 50 whenever p′ = 0.
Operational quantitiesE′, p′, relative speed and chiral fractions update live from p′ = γ(p − βE), E′ = γ(E − βp), PR,L = (1±β′)/2 = (E′±p′c)/2E′ with E′ = √((p′c)²+(mₑc²)²).

Guided Inquiry

1 · One electron, two arrows

Let’s meet our electron, with momentum 1 MeV/c. The purple arrow is its spin S, and the lower arrow is its momentum p′ in your frame. Helicity h = S·p̂ compares the two: right now they’re aligned, so h starts at +½ħ.

2 · Overtake it

Now you’re going to overtake this electron, and the spin arrow won’t turn. What do you think happens to helicity h = S·p̂?

3 · Chirality ≠ helicity

So once you’ve overtaken it, h = −½ħ. Now for chirality, which is often called Lorentz-invariant. Which control(s) do you think change the R : L mix?

4 · The massless limit

One last chase. At p = 20 MeV/c, even β = 0.9 leaves you behind. What do you think helicity will do at the boost slider’s far end?

Here’s the big payoff: a massless particle can never be overtaken, so its helicity is absolute and equals its chirality — that’s what a left-handed neutrino means.

01

At a glance

This sim puts one electron on screen and lets you change who is watching it. It shows how the electron's helicity, momentum and chirality look from different frames, which is why "left-handed" means different things for a particle with mass and one without.

What you'll learn

  • What helicity compares, and where the observer's frame enters.
  • How the electron's momentum p and your boost β set the numbers in the readouts.
  • What chirality is, and how it differs from helicity.
  • What "left-handed" means for a particle with mass and for one without.
One electron, its spin S, and its momentum p′ as the observer measures it. The observer moves along the electron's line of motion.

What's on screen

  • Spin S (purple arrow) and the ball's rotation: fixed in direction and sense.
  • p′ (arrow below the ball): the momentum in the observer's frame. Green points right, orange left. Its length is on a compressed scale, so keV/c and MeV/c both fit.
  • Chips at the top: the boost β (left) and the helicity h (right).
  • Chirality bar (bottom): the R-chiral (green) and L-chiral (orange) shares, with percentages.
  • Readouts (sidebar): E′, p′, h, the electron's speed in your frame, and R : L.
See itStart from the lab frame with p = 1 MeV/c. Watch for: the spin arrow above the ball and the p′ arrow below it pointing the same way, with h = +½ħ.

03

Helicity compares two arrows

Helicity is the component of the spin along the direction of motion: h = S·p̂, where p̂ is the unit vector along the momentum as the observer measures it. For an electron it has two possible values, +½ħ (spin along the momentum) or −½ħ (spin against it).

  • The purple arrow is S. The arrow below the ball is p′, and the colour of both p′ and the helicity chip shows the sign of h: green for +½ħ, orange for −½ħ.
  • The observer moves along the line of the electron's motion. A boost along that line does not change the spin component along it, so the sim keeps S and the ball's rotation sense fixed.
  • The electron's own numbers at p = 1 MeV/c: E = √(p²c² + (mₑc²)²) = 1.123 MeV, and its speed is pc/E = 0.890 c. In the lab frame, the "speed in frame" readout shows that 0.890 c.
See itSweep the boost from 0 to 0.9. Watch for: the purple spin arrow and the ball's rotation staying as they are while the p′ arrow changes.
04

Why overtaking flips helicity

Boosting along p gives p′ = γ(p − βE). Factoring out E shows the whole story, with βp = p/E the electron's own speed in the lab (c = 1):

The sign of p′, and so the sign of h, is set by whether your β is below or above βp.
  • Below βp you are chasing the electron and p′ points forward: h = +½ħ. Above it you have overtaken it, p′ points backward and h = −½ħ. The spin never moved; the direction it is compared with did.
  • p′ passes through zero smoothly. h is the sign of p′, so it jumps. At p′ = 0 the electron is at rest in your frame and h is undefined (the sim shows this for |β′| < 0.004).
  • At p = 1 MeV/c the flip is at β = 0.890, the tick under the β slider. At β = 0.9, p′ = −24.5 keV/c.
p′ against β for p = 1 MeV/c, and the helicity it implies.
p β

These sliders move the sim too.

See itGlide β slowly across the flip point at p = 1 MeV/c. Watch for: p′ shrinking steadily through zero, while the helicity chip jumps from +½ħ to −½ħ.
05

Chirality is a separate label

Chirality labels the two parts of the electron's field, R-chiral and L-chiral. The weak force acts on the L-chiral part only. Chirality does not depend on the frame: a state that is purely L-chiral is purely L-chiral for every observer.

For an electron with mass, helicity and chirality do not line up. A state of definite helicity is a mixture of both chiralities, and the chirality bar shows the shares:

β′ = p′c/E′ is the electron's signed speed in the observer's frame (the "speed in frame" readout).
  • The mixture depends on β′, which depends on both p and β. In the lab at p = 1 MeV/c the bar reads 94.5 : 5.5. At β = 0.9 it reads 47.6 : 52.4.
  • At p′ = 0 the bar reads 50 : 50. An electron at rest has no preferred handedness.
  • The bar's green and orange are R and L chirality. They are a different quantity from the green and orange of the helicity chip.
See itRide along with the electron at p = 1 MeV/c. Watch for: the chirality bar at 50 : 50 and the helicity chip reading "undefined".
See itCompare the lab-frame bar at p = 0.1 and at 20 MeV/c. Watch for: the card showing both R : L readings side by side.
06

Massless particles have no flip

For m = 0 the flip point is at β = 1, which no observer reaches.
  • A massless particle travels at c in every frame, so no observer gets ahead of it. Its helicity never changes sign, and its chirality is the same in every frame. For such a particle helicity and chirality are the same label.
  • "Left-handed neutrino" is a statement about chirality. Only for a massless particle can you read it as negative helicity.
  • The sim's electron has mass, so it only approaches this limit. The flip is reachable only if βp ≤ 0.9995, which means p ≲ 16 MeV/c. At p = 20 MeV/c, βp = 0.99967 is past the end of the slider.
The same speeds on a rapidity axis, so the crowd near β = 1 is readable.

The electron still has mass, so the bar is not pinned. At p = 20 MeV/c and β = 0.9995, p′ stays positive, but the electron's speed in your frame is only 0.21 c and the bar reads 60.5 : 39.5.

See itSet p = 20 MeV/c and push the boost to the end of the slider. Watch for: p′ staying positive and h = +½ħ, with the bar well short of 100 % R.
07

Where it matters

  • Beta decay. The weak force acts on L-chiral fields. A left-chiral electron has helicity −½ħ with probability (1 + β)/2, so electrons from β decay have a longitudinal polarisation of −v/c. These are the same (1 ± β)/2 weights as the bar, read the other way round.
  • Pion decay. A pion has spin 0, so in π− → ℓ− ν̄ the lepton leaves with the antineutrino's helicity, +½ħ. Its L-chiral share is (1 − β)/2: 0.36 for the muon, 1.3 × 10−5 for the electron. This helicity suppression is behind the measured ratio Γ(π → eν) / Γ(π → μν) = 1.2 × 10−4.
  • High-energy collisions. For E ≫ mc² helicity and chirality nearly coincide, so helicity is the standard label for particles in a collision.
The L-chiral share of an h = +½ħ lepton against its momentum; the shaded band is the range of the p slider.
Go deeper: antiparticles and neutrino mass
The L-chiral share of an h = +½ħ lepton, and its high-energy limit.
  • A left-chiral field creates a left-handed particle but a right-handed antiparticle, in the massless limit. That is why the ν̄ above has h = +½ħ.
  • Neutrinos have a small mass, so strictly their helicity is not absolute: a left-chiral neutrino of energy E has a positive-helicity share of about (mc²/2E)², far too small to detect at the energies of any beam.
08

Summary

In one line. Helicity compares a spin that does not change with a momentum that depends on the observer, so for a massive particle it can flip; chirality is the label that does not.

Key points

  • h = S·p̂ is ±½ħ. A boost along p leaves S alone and changes p′.
  • p′ = γE(βp − β): h changes sign at β = βp = p/E, jumps, and is undefined at p′ = 0.
  • Chirality is the same in every frame. A helicity state's R : L shares, (1 ± β′)/2, are not.
  • For m = 0 there is no flip, and helicity and chirality coincide.

Common mix-ups

  • "Helicity is intrinsic, like spin." Not for anything with mass. The spin never moved; the momentum direction did.
  • "h fades smoothly through zero as you catch up." p′ does. h is its sign, so it jumps, with one undefined instant.
  • "Left-chiral means negative helicity." Only when E ≫ mₑc², and for a particle, not an antiparticle.

Things to try on your own

  • Set p to 0.1 MeV/c and check the marker under the β slider against p/E = 0.192.
  • At p = 1 MeV/c press ride along, then step β by 0.0005 each way. Count the steps for which h reads "undefined".
  • At p = 5 MeV/c, read R : L at β = 0.9. Then at β = 0, find the p that gives the same bar, and compare it with the p′ you saw.
